item.title: Mortgage Rates Rise Slightly to 7.09% APR Today
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Mortgage Rates Today, Thursday, November 12: A Little Higher
Mortgage rates rose slightly to 7.09% APR today, up nine basis points from yesterday and 13 basis points from a week ago. The increase follows the Bureau of Labor Statistics reporting 0.4% inflation in October, exceeding forecasts. The Federal Reserve’s anticipated December rate hike and potential January hikes could further pressure rates. While current rates remain above the 2% target, investors are uncertain if additional hikes will curb inflation. Homeowners may consider refinancing if their current rates are 7.59% or higher, though breaking even on closing costs requires staying in the home long enough. Lenders adjust rates daily based on market conditions, so locking in a rate is advisable if a favorable deal is secured. Personalized quotes vary due to factors like credit scores and down payments, making it crucial to compare offers and understand affordability before committing.

item.title: New Brain Atlas Reveals Disease-Linked Cells and Therapies
item.description:
Source: FT News Feed Original headline: New brain atlas promises disease breakthroughs
Scientists created the largest multi-species brain atlas of the basal ganglia, a region vital for movement, emotions, and decision-making. The research, involving over 500 scientists from nine countries, mapped 25.5 million cells from humans, macaques, marmosets, and mice. Findings include a new cell type linked to schizophrenia risk, a modified gene therapy for Parkinson’s that reduces tremors in animals, and genetic connections to autism. The atlas also reveals how gene expression changes with aging. Evan Macosko of Harvard Medical School called the basal ganglia the 'grand central' for brain diseases, emphasizing the need for a detailed map to understand and treat disorders. Hongkui Zeng of the Allen Institute noted the importance of cell-type-specific gene analysis for disease research. Frank Hirth of King’s College London described the region as essential for movement and sensory awareness. Researchers stress the need for further studies to validate molecular findings and their impact on brain health.

item.title: Ukrainian drone strikes Russian warship in Gulf of Finland
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
A Russian warship was attacked by Ukrainian drones in the Gulf of Finland, marking the first such strike in a Baltic Sea area open to civilian traffic. Finnish officials confirmed the incident, with Ukraine's SBU claiming the attack targeted the Naro-Fominsk corvette as part of a broader operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil terminal. The strike occurred in a narrow waterway used by oil tankers and subsea cables. Estonia's defense minister reported the attack happened around 05:30, noting smoke from the ship and its retreat toward St. Petersburg. Details on casualties or damage remain unclear. Military analyst Emil Kastehelmi noted the strike did not signal significant escalation. Ukrainian drones also targeted the Ust-Luga region overnight, with some crossing into Estonian airspace briefly. NATO aircraft were present but did not engage drones. Ukraine denied using Baltic states' airspace for attacks, citing Russian electronic warfare interference.

item.title: EU Leaders Hold First AI Summit Amid Global Tech Concerns
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: EU leaders gather for first ever AI summit
European Union leaders meet in Dublin for the first AI summit, addressing the technology's impact on economies and societies. European Council President Antonio Costa emphasized the need for leaders' level discussion on AI's opportunities and risks. The summit, held at Dublin's Convention Center, features speeches from French AI firm Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch and researcher Geoffrey Hinton. Concerns about AI's potential harm, including recent incidents involving rogue AI agents and scrutiny of tech leaders like Nvidia's Jensen Huang, frame the event. Estonia and Finland urge EU-level frameworks to manage AI risks, while Mistral advocates for continued advancement. Leaders debate Europe's role in the AI race, balancing innovation with safeguards against risks to individuals and businesses.

item.title: US Army Awards $2.5M Contract for AI Drones to Protect Abrams Tanks
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: The US Army is putting money on AI drones that can find hidden threats and protect its Abrams tanks
The US Army has awarded a $2.5 million contract to Safe Pro Group to integrate its Ground Truth threat-detection software into Anduril Industries' Ghost-X drone. The software, built on Ukrainian battlefield data, identifies over 150 explosive threats and enemy drones from aerial imagery. It aims to protect Abrams tanks by mapping land mines, anti-personnel mines, cluster munitions, and first-person-view ambush drones. The contract reflects the Army's shift in tactics amid evolving threats like aerial drones and ground robots. Ukrainian battlefields, with dense minefields and FPV drones, have highlighted the need for improved situational awareness. The Ghost-X drones will use AI to detect threats and share data via military networks like ATAK and Lattice. Daniel Leighton of Anduril Industries stated the technology enhances tank survivability and reconnaissance by providing faster, reliable threat detection at the tactical edge.

item.title: San Diego, Chula Vista Push Resolutions Against SDG&E Rate Hike, Municipal Utility Plans
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: A pair of city resolutions take shots at SDG&E. Will they have much impact?
Two city resolutions target SDG&E as San Diego’s Environment Committee passed a resolution supporting a municipal utility and Chula Vista Mayor John McCann introduced a measure opposing a proposed rate hike. SDG&E seeks approval for an 8% revenue increase, which would raise typical residential bills by 8.5% compared to 2027. McCann called the hike a burden on families, while Shane Harris of the San Diego Public Advocate argued resolutions commit cities to lobbying against the proposal. San Diego’s resolution emphasizes affordability, local control, and worker protections, with Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera stating residents are ‘fed up’ with SDG&E. A 2022 study suggested a municipal utility could save $600 million over 30 years but warned of theoretical assumptions. SDG&E’s Brittany Applestein Syz countered that public power would initially raise bills and delay savings. The resolution passed 2-1, with Councilmember Jennifer Campbell arguing focus should remain on the California Public Utilities Commission. Meanwhile, San Francisco faces its own utility disputes, with PG&E disputing the city’s infrastructure valuation. The CPUC plans to rule on SDG&E’s rate case by late 2024.

item.title: Community Colleges Expand Semiconductor Training to Address Labor Shortage
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Community colleges rush to expand semiconductor training as labor shortage looms US chip industry
Community colleges are expanding semiconductor training programs to address a labor shortage in the U.S. chip industry. Ethan Mock, a 23-year-old student, enrolled in a free, three-month course at Rio Salado College, which connects students with major chipmakers like TSMC and Intel. The program, part of a broader initiative under the 2022 CHIPS Act, aims to fill entry-level roles such as technicians, with 75% of graduates securing semiconductor-related jobs. Shari Liss of SEMI warned of a potential 157,000 worker shortage by 2030, particularly in states like Texas, Ohio, and Arizona. Colleges like Rio Salado and Austin Community College are offering accelerated, hands-on training in clean-room labs, often funded by industry partners. Rick Vaughn of Rio Salado noted that these programs avoid student debt and provide a credible path into the industry. Meanwhile, companies like TSMC are investing billions in U.S. plants, bringing in international engineers to support local hiring. TSMC’s Phoenix project, the largest foreign investment in U.S. history, aims to create 25,000 jobs, half locally. Experts stress the need for precision and safety in training, as the industry shifts from Asia to America.

item.title: Colleges offer free tuition for low-income families to simplify cost confusion
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: The cost of college is confusing. Some schools are trying to change that
Middlebury College and other institutions are offering tuition-free enrollment for families with incomes up to $175,000, aiming to simplify college cost confusion. Middlebury’s policy, effective next year, covers 35-50 students annually, though most families earning that income already attend tuition-free. Experts say the goal is to address widespread public frustration over opaque pricing. Nearly 80% of families eliminate schools based on cost, per a Sallie Mae survey. Schools like Princeton, MIT, and Harvard set similar income thresholds, but most aren’t lowering prices—just clarifying costs. Phillip Levine, an economist, notes that advertised prices are rarely paid, creating misperceptions. Colleges often delay final cost disclosures until after acceptance, complicating financial decisions. Parents compare the process to medical billing, where costs are unclear until final approval. Free-tuition guarantees don’t cover room, board, or other expenses, though aid is available. Over 70% of students and parents find financial aid confusing, and nearly two-thirds view four-year colleges as unaffordable. Colleges increasingly advertise high list prices, then offer discounts, leaving most students paying less than listed amounts. Middlebury’s president, Ian Baucom, emphasizes transparency, calling it essential for informed financial choices. Other schools, like the University of Pennsylvania, are introducing calculators to pre-estimate costs. Institutions with fewer resources offer limited free-tuition programs, such as Earlham College for Indiana residents or Wake Forest for in-state students. The push for clarity aims to rebuild trust in higher education amid rising costs and economic uncertainty.

item.title: AI Predicts PTSD Risk, Exoplanet Found, Sleep Affects Cybersecurity
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Original headline: This week in science: PTSD prediction, phishing while tired, an exoplanet
Researchers developed an AI model that predicts PTSD risk in trauma patients by analyzing their emergency room narratives, achieving 95% accuracy. The model, described in Nature Communications, uses patients' own words to identify future PTSD risk, offering a streamlined alternative to manual assessments. Psychologist Katharina Schultebraucks emphasized the model's potential to guide early interventions, though privacy concerns were addressed through HIPAA-compliant data handling. A separate study confirmed a new technique to detect exoplanets by subtracting stellar light from images, revealing 51 Eridani b. Published in Nature, the method improves detection of faint planets by correcting telescope errors and instrumental issues. Meanwhile, a cybersecurity study found that sleep-deprived individuals were 13% more likely to fall for phishing attacks after daylight saving time transitions, with results published in PNAS. Sleep specialist Muhammad Adeel Rishi linked DST to increased health risks, urging cybersecurity firms to adjust protocols during sleep-loss events.

item.title: Bring out your umbrellas. Cooling temperatures and scattered showers start Thursday night
item.description:
Source: LA Times
A Pacific storm system will bring rain to much of California starting Thursday evening, with a second storm expected Sunday. Rainfall will focus on Northern California, with scattered showers in Southern California. Climate scientist Daniel Swain noted the rain will add to above-average totals but won’t be a dramatic winter storm. Cooler temperatures, dropping 10 degrees in the evening, are expected from an offshore pattern shifting onshore. Highs will range from mid-70s to low 80s, with overnight lows in the mid-60s. Winds of 20-35 mph will gust across Los Angeles County Friday. Rain is anticipated to begin after 10 p.m. Thursday in Santa Barbara County and after midnight in Los Angeles County, with widespread rainfall late Friday into Saturday. Totals could reach a quarter-inch to an inch. Minor flood advisories are possible. A second storm on Sunday may strengthen due to record-warm ocean waters, increasing thunderstorm potential. High surf advisories will remain Friday through Tuesday, with surf heights up to 12 feet on west-facing beaches. Swimmers are warned about rip currents and to follow lifeguard guidance.

item.title: Instacart partners with Provi to deliver non-alcoholic supplies to bars and restaurants
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Instacart wants to deliver supplies to your favorite bar or restaurant
Instacart has partnered with Provi, a B2B alcohol marketplace, to offer same-day delivery of non-alcoholic items like mixers and paper products to bars and restaurants. The collaboration excludes alcohol due to U.S. three-tier distribution laws. Provi CEO Matthew Tucker said the partnership addresses last-minute stock shortages, such as extra limes or napkins. Instacart's Andrew Nodes noted the move expands the company's business-to-business offerings, allowing restaurants to avoid service disruptions. The partnership launches during peak demand for Provi's platform, coinciding with Thanksgiving and Christmas. Provi users can order through their app and redirect to Instacart for delivery. Tucker highlighted that garnishes and supplies are critical for high-margin drinks, and labor shortages exacerbate the need for quick restocking. 'If you don't have the garnishes, you aren't able to sell some of your highest-margin products,' he said.

item.title: Graffiti Removed from LA's Oceanwide Plaza Towers
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Notorious Graffiti Towers wiped clean in downtown Los Angeles
Crews removed graffiti from Oceanwide Plaza towers in downtown Los Angeles, a stalled $1.2-billion real estate project. City officials and buyers KPC Group and Lendlease prioritized the cleanup ahead of the 2028 Olympics, with removal mandated as part of the bankruptcy sale closing in January. The project, 60% complete when developer Oceanwide Holdings collapsed in 2019, requires an additional $850 million to finish. Graffiti, applied by taggers and daredevils, was scrubbed with biodegradable solution, though some window paint remains. KPC executive John Petty called the cleanup a 'renaissance' for the area, aiming to transform the site into a luxury residential, hotel, and retail complex. Councilwoman Ysabel Jurado praised the effort as a step toward realizing the project’s potential for housing, jobs, and economic growth. Developers plan to rename the site and add a massive electronic sign to its facade before the Olympics.

item.title: US jobless claims rise to 200,000 but stay near historic lows
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Original headline: US jobless claims tick up to 200,000 but remain low by historic standards
US jobless claims rose to 200,000 last week, surpassing the 195,000 forecast, but remain historically low. The four-week average of claims stayed at 195,250, reflecting continued job market stability. Applications for unemployment benefits, a proxy for layoffs, have not exceeded 230,000 in any week this year and have been below 200,000 for nine consecutive weeks. Employers added an average of 86,000 jobs monthly in 2024, including a strong 165,000 last month, compared to a sluggish 9,700 average in 2025. Consumer spending has remained resilient, and increased investment in artificial intelligence has supported economic growth. Despite the slight rise in claims, the labor market shows few signs of distress, with layoffs rare and job security unusually high.

item.title: Ukraine Reports Starlink Restrictions Amid US-Moscow Talks
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Ukraine says Starlink restrictions are back as US envoys land in Moscow
Ukraine reports renewed speed restrictions on Starlink military service as US envoys meet Putin. President Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces face significant disruptions to Starshield, the Pentagon-funded satellite service, with speed capped at 161kph (100mph) over front lines and occupied areas. He called the restrictions a deliberate tactic to aid Russian drone attacks. US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Putin in Moscow, with Kyiv alleging Washington is strengthening Russia’s position. The European Commission condemned the restrictions as unacceptable, urging SpaceX to restore services. Zelenskyy accused Trump and Musk of undermining Ukraine’s defenses, though neither provided explanations. Russia insists on territorial gains, with Putin demanding Ukraine surrender Donbas and southern regions. Medinsky called for a new European security system, framing Russia’s claims as non-negotiable. European leaders warn of being trapped into discussing broader security frameworks to participate in peace talks.

item.title: Huge Surf Threatens Coastal Flooding in San Diego County
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Huge surf could cause coastal flooding this weekend at San Diego County beaches
A large west-northwest swell will produce 10-foot waves this weekend in San Diego County, causing coastal flooding from Oceanside to Imperial Beach. Forecasters warn the El Niño-enhanced storm, arriving Friday, will coincide with rain until late Saturday and possible thunderstorms. San Diego could see half an inch of rain by Sunday, when largest waves hit, creating dangerous rip currents. Tides near 7 feet may combine with high surf to cause localized erosion and overflow into parking lots and boardwalks. The region faces one of its wettest winters on record due to El Niño, with sea surface temperatures unusually warm. Marine heat waves have contributed to coastal kelp decline, with La Jolla Cove surf temperatures at 75.2°F, 11°F above normal. Scientists note warm waters may persist through late winter, threatening kelp forests critical to marine ecosystems and industries like pharmaceuticals, food, and cosmetics.

item.title: AWS CEO doubts space data centers' viability in next decade
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: AWS CEO throws cold water on AI data centers in space
AWS CEO Matt Garman doubts the feasibility of space-based data centers, calling them 'highly unlikely' to be economically viable in the next decade. He highlighted the high cost of rocket launches and challenges in dissipating heat in space, noting that 'dissipating heat in space is actually quite hard.' Garman contrasted space with underwater data centers, which he also deemed impractical, and suggested deserts as a more viable option due to their environmental advantages. While Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos have supported space-based data centers, Garman emphasized that 'these are all technically solvable problems' but would take time. He also addressed concerns about water use, stating Amazon's largest data centers use less water than 40 US households. Garman acknowledged the potential economic benefits of data centers but warned that remote locations could miss out on tax revenue and jobs.

item.title: Frontier Launches First-Class Seats at $129
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Frontier is now offering first-class seats starting at $129
Frontier Airlines is introducing first-class seating on select flights starting March 5, 2027. The new first-class section, located in the first two rows, features a seat pitch of 37 inches—wider than Frontier’s usual 28-31 inches—and a 2-by-2 seating arrangement without middle seats. Individual USB-C power ports will be added, alongside Starlink Wi-Fi, which will roll out incrementally across aircraft in 2027. First-class seats do not include meals or snacks unless purchased separately. The airline also offers extra-legroom seats with 34-inch pitch and USB ports, priced at $90 one-way. A promotional period for bookings before November 17 offers discounted fares for travel through April 5. Frontier’s move follows JetBlue’s announcement of its Bluefirst premium class, which includes meals and wider reclining seats. Frontier, based in Denver, has faced poor performance rankings in recent years but continues to expand its services.

item.title: California Beaches Closed Over E. coli Outbreaks
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Popular California beach closed amid E. coli outbreak
Santa Cruz County closed Capitola Beach after nine children contracted E. coli linked to the area or nearby waterways. Health officials tested water at four locations, including Soquel Creek and Monterey Bay, as visitors and pets were warned to avoid contact with ocean, creek, and lagoon water. Four children in Santa Cruz County and five from other Bay Area counties were affected. The closure follows a separate E. coli outbreak in San Luis Obispo County, where one person died and over a dozen visitors to Brookshire Farms reported symptoms. Health officials confirmed the death and noted testing of food, water, and samples at the farm did not find the specific strain. San Luis Obispo County Health Officer Dr. Christy Mulkerin stated the risk of additional exposure had passed, though the exact source remains undetermined. Brookshire Farms temporarily closed during pumpkin season, and the city canceled its Pumpkin Smash event. Officials emphasized that while environmental testing failed to identify the source, clinical data pointed to a short-lived shared exposure.

item.title: European leaders reject Russian security overhaul push
item.description:
Source: FT News Feed Original headline: European leaders reject Russian push to overhaul continent’s security
European leaders have rejected Russia’s proposal to overhaul the continent’s security architecture, as part of ongoing Ukraine peace talks. Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin and foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov, have pushed for a new security framework, demanding a ban on NATO expansion, military drills near Russia’s borders, and troop withdrawals from NATO’s eastern flank. European leaders, including President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warned that such discussions risk diverting attention from achieving a ceasefire in Ukraine. Zelenskyy said talks between the U.S. and Russia on security guarantees were ‘more about a new framework between Europe and Russia’ than Ukraine. European Council President António Costa called Russia’s invasion the reason the existing security system collapsed. Putin argued that security discussions should occur after a peace deal, while Ushakov emphasized the need for a ‘non-nuclear security and peace’ architecture. EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas stated Europe should only engage in security talks after Russia agrees to a peace deal. Leaders expressed concern that participating in broader security discussions could compromise NATO sovereignty, with Estonia’s PM Kristen Michal warning of a ‘trap’ for Europe.

item.title: Three Killed in Wrong-Way Freeway Crash Near Riverside
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Three dead in early-morning wrong-way crash in Riverside
Three people died in a head-on collision on the westbound 91 Freeway in Riverside early Thursday morning after a driver entered the wrong lane, according to the California Highway Patrol. Incident logs state the driver was heading eastbound in the westbound lanes near 14th Street, swerving between cars in the second and third lanes. The crash involved a white SUV turned on its side, a big rig leaking fluid, and a damaged black sedan identified as a BMW. One additional person was hospitalized in unknown condition. CHP officers arrived around 2 a.m. to the scene, which prompted immediate lane closures on the freeway. All westbound lanes near 14th Street were closed by 4:30 a.m., with traffic fully reopened by 8:39 a.m. A Riverside County spokesperson confirmed the wrong-way driver struck the big rig, with a third vehicle involved in the collision. The California Highway Patrol is investigating the incident.

item.title: San Marcos City Council delays vote on 31-unit condo project
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego
The San Marcos City Council postponed a vote on a 31-unit condominium project in San Elijo Hills. Council members raised concerns about the fire protection plan during Tuesday's meeting. Veronica Alarid, a resident and Prado II HOA vice president, supports the delay, citing traffic congestion and safety risks. 'I have literally seen it become like a recipe of disaster,' Alarid said, describing the area's existing traffic issues. Council member Mike Sannella questioned the developer's approach, asking why the fire plan wasn't adjusted. Developer Robert Honer claimed they consulted city departments and believed their plan was sufficient. The developer has not commented on the latest delay but previously expressed optimism about construction starting a year after approval. Residents like Alarid continue to oppose the project, seeking alternative outcomes.

item.title: U.S. Seizes $1.2 Billion from Binance Hack, Dismantles $400M Crypto Scam
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle, San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: U.S. Seizes $1.2 Billion from Binance Hack as FBI Unveils North Korea's $400M Crypto Scam
U.S. authorities seized $1.2 billion from a Binance hack and dismantled a $400 million crypto scam linked to North Korea. The FBI and Justice Department announced the actions, targeting two cyberattacks attributed to North Korean hackers. The Binance breach, executed by TraderTraitor in October, involved stealing $6.3 billion, with over $2.7 billion frozen. A separate scheme, FaceStealer, used fake video calls and AI-generated deepfakes to defraud 900 victims in the crypto and web3 sectors. Hackers mimicked trusted contacts via Zoom and Teams, using pre-recorded videos and malicious links to access contact lists. The FBI linked the attack to the Sapphire Sleet hacking cluster, while officials stated North Korea uses cryptocurrency theft to fund its regime. FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman and Justice Department’s M. Scott Proctor confirmed the link to North Korea’s cyber operations, despite Pyongyang denying involvement. Authorities seized 900 webcam videos and disrupted cloud infrastructure used by the hackers.
item.source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle, San Diego Union-Tribune

item.title: Turkey Challenges Seabed Cable Project Amid Maritime Disputes
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Original headline: The Coming Era of Undersea Anarchy
Turkey opposes the Great Sea Interconnector (GSI), a seabed power cable linking Greece and Cyprus, citing territorial claims in the Aegean. Ankara, a non-ratifier of UNCLOS, argues the project infringes on its exclusive economic zone. Greece and Cyprus seek the cable to reduce fossil fuel dependence, but Turkey demands control, proposing instead a gas pipeline to Cyprus. The dispute highlights broader maritime disputes, with Turkey challenging UNCLOS norms by asserting sovereignty over disputed waters. Similar issues exist globally: China enforces permits in the South China Sea, Russia violates UNCLOS with its fleet, and the U.S. recently allowed unilateral mining in international waters. Cable firms face legal uncertainty, as Turkey insists on notices for GSI activities, potentially delaying the project. The conflict underscores a shift toward maritime anarchy, as nations prioritize national interests over international law. The GSI symbolizes a larger trend of contested seabed claims, with Turkey seeking to redefine maritime boundaries in its favor.

item.title: Italian schools face second day of bomb hoax threats
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
Italian schools faced bomb threats for a second consecutive day, prompting evacuations of 1,800 institutions across the country. The threats, similar to those causing chaos on Wednesday, included a mass email signed by 'Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan,' though no devices were found. The Italian government advised against evacuations without concrete evidence. Similar threats were reported in Scotland, Northern Ireland, and France, where a Calais rail station alert disrupted train services. Officials suspect the threats may originate from Taiwan or a hacked Philippine teacher account. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called the incidents a strategy to cause alarm. Parents and protesters, including those against a Rome school headmaster who dismissed the threats as fake, demand clearer government action and national guidelines. The threats were later denied by the alleged group, which previously claimed responsibility for other hoaxes in Europe.

item.title: TFFF Rainforest Fund Aims to Raise $10 Billion by 2026
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Is the TFFF rainforest fund failing due to a lack of money?
The Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) aims to protect rainforests by raising $10 billion in government loans and $100 billion from private investors by 2026. The fund will pay countries $4 per hectare preserved, but only for intact ecosystems, with 20% allocated to Indigenous communities. Satellite monitoring ensures compliance, and funds are protected by government guarantees. Norway, Brazil, Indonesia, and others have pledged support, but only $7.9 billion is confirmed. Felix Finkbeiner, founder of Plant-for-the-Planet, emphasized that TFFF offers countries more sovereignty than traditional financing, as funds remain in the pool for 40 years. Deforestation in the Amazon dropped 41% between 2025-2026, but global losses remain high. The fund will invest in green bonds, avoiding climate-harming projects. Finkbeiner remains optimistic about securing the remaining $2.1 billion by COP31, with Norway’s $3 billion pledge conditional on meeting the deadline.

item.title: Brooklyn building collapse kills eight, including two children
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Original headline: What we know about victims of deadly Brooklyn building collapse
A three-story building in Brooklyn collapsed into a construction site, killing eight people including two children aged 9 and 10. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani identified the victims as friends, neighbors, and immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Trinidad, and other countries. Two were construction workers. Eighteen others were injured, including four firefighters, with one remaining in critical condition. The collapse near Flatbush and Bedford Avenues destroyed part of an adjacent building, prompting a rescue operation. Six victims were declared dead at the scene, two later died in the hospital. Authorities praised first responders, including construction workers who rescued others. Rescue efforts ended Thursday afternoon after no further survivors were found. The mayor highlighted the heroism of those involved in the rescue.

item.title: Atmospheric Rivers Cause Flooding in Pacific Northwest
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: Rivers in the sky are raining down on the Pacific Northwest. What are they?
Atmospheric rivers are causing heavy rain and flooding in the Pacific Northwest. Two storms are set to hit Oregon and Washington on Friday and Saturday, following earlier rainfall. Meteorologist Josh Weiss warns of compounding impacts from multiple atmospheric rivers, including flash flooding, urban flooding, and landslides. These narrow bands of moisture, up to 2,000 miles long, contribute 50-60% of California's rain. UCSD's F. Martin Ralph notes 90% of Western U.S. flood damage comes from atmospheric rivers. El Niño's warm waters may fuel storms but do not strengthen atmospheric rivers, according to Ralph's research. Rising sea levels and King tides increase coastal flooding risks. The term, popularized by social media, refers to weather patterns like Pineapple Express. Scientists stress the need to monitor these events regardless of El Niño or La Niña phases. Residents face significant swells and flood risks this weekend.

item.title: Can green cement decarbonise the data centre building boom?
item.description:
Source: FT World
Meta is backing Sublime Systems to produce low-carbon cement, aiming to reduce emissions from its data centre construction. The tech giant will purchase 180,000 tonnes of cement via environmental attribute certificates, which allow it to claim carbon reductions without using the physical material. Cement accounts for 7% of global CO₂ emissions due to kiln operations and limestone processing. Sublime’s electrochemical method produces 70-80% less CO₂ than traditional cement, costing $160-$180 per tonne. Critics argue certificates enable greenwashing by allowing companies to offset emissions without reducing actual output. Sublime denies this, stating the deal funds real low-carbon production. The company plans a 150,000-200,000 tonne plant, with potential expansion to 1 million tonnes annually. Meta also retains the option to buy physical cement if a nearby plant is built. Sublime aims to scale beyond data centres, targeting schools, hospitals, and infrastructure projects. The deal follows Microsoft’s 2025 agreement for similar certificates, highlighting growing corporate interest in decarbonising construction materials.
